meta.title: Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation Vol. 23
meta.blurb: A green-haired baby, a journey to the Divine Continent, and a hunt for the Second Eye of the Demon Continent.
meta.author: Rifujin na Magonote
meta.notes: Extracted from the user's EPUB for a personal reading edition.
meta.attribution: Speaker labels were assigned by contextual review, page by page. Diary excerpts, remembered quotations, imagined speech, and narration containing quoted fragments are distinguished from live dialogue.

scenes.location: Rudeus's house, Sharia (Sylphiette's bedroom)

blocks.text: I HAD A DREAM once. It was around the time that Rudy went to the King Dragon Realm. In my dream, there was a child crying. A group of dark shadows surrounded her. They ganged up on the child and threw pitch-black lumps of something at her. The child desperately tried to run away, but the shadows would always follow.
blocks.html: I HAD A DREAM once. It was around the time that Rudy went to the King Dragon Realm. In my dream, there was a child crying. A group of dark shadows surrounded her. They ganged up on the child and threw pitch-black lumps of something at her. The child desperately tried to run away, but the shadows would always follow.

blocks.text: The child ran toward a light. As she approached the light, it tossed balls of light at the shadows, and they dispersed. The light then gently enveloped the child as she drifted off to sleep.
blocks.html: The child ran toward a light. As she approached the light, it tossed balls of light at the shadows, and they dispersed. The light then gently enveloped the child as she drifted off to sleep.

blocks.text: When I first had that dream, I thought it was about the past. A dream about the old days when the village kids would bully me. I believed I was dreaming about it after all this time as a sign of how much I loved Rudy. That was all I thought of as I lay back down and wriggled happily, like a little girl.

I believed I was dreaming about it after all this time as a sign of how much I loved Rudy. That was all I thought of as I lay back down and wriggled happily, like a little girl.

blocks.text: Several months later, around the time when Rudy was off in the Demon Continent, I had another dream just like it. This time, it went differently.
blocks.html: Several months later, around the time when Rudy was off in the Demon Continent, I had another dream just like it. This time, it went differently.

blocks.text: The green-haired child was here. But instead of having my face, the child now had Rudy’s. The green-haired child with Rudy’s face was being chased by dark shadows. There was no light where the child was headed. I panicked and dashed up to the child, desperate to protect him from the shadows. Without my magic, I could only try and swat the shadows away with my bare hands. The shadows were tenacious. They refused to stay away. I could feel the child shuddering in my arms.

blocks.text: After this dream, I worried that some harm might have come to Rudy. Maybe he’d been injured or captured. No, of course not. He had Eris and Roxy with him…

blocks.text: I thought long and hard about what to do to help, and in the end, I returned home that very day. It calmed my worries about my husband…but new worries sprung up in their place.

blocks.text: My tummy had grown round and big. What if that dream was about the child inside it?
blocks.html: My tummy had grown round and big. What if that dream was about the child inside it?

blocks.text: I was fretting over nothing, I quickly told myself. There was no way that Rudy wouldn’t protect our child. There had to be a light awaiting them. I convinced myself that the pregnancy nerves were just getting to me. I put the dream out of my mind.

blocks.text: Eventually, Rudy returned from the Demon Continent. I asked about a name for the baby. It had now been six months since he told me he’d “think one up.” I could have waited for it until after I gave birth, but I said I wanted to know in advance in case he left soon on another trip.

blocks.text: “I’m sorry. I still haven’t thought about the name.”
blocks.html: “I’m sorry. I still haven’t thought about the name.”

blocks.text: That moment, the thought of that dream flitted across my mind. The vision of that child surrounded by dark shadows with nobody to help him. Then, a worse one: Did Rudy love this child?
blocks.html: That moment, the thought of that dream flitted across my mind. The vision of that child surrounded by dark shadows with nobody to help him. Then, a worse one: Did Rudy love this child?

blocks.text: Of course he did. I was sure of it. That night, however, I had the dream again. The shadows gathered around the child, who was far beyond my reach. I ran as fast as I could to help…but I didn’t make it. When I reached the child, I found that the shadows had gone…and that the child was dead.

I ran as fast as I could to help…but I didn’t make it. When I reached the child, I found that the shadows had gone…and that the child was dead.

blocks.text: I woke up drenched in sweat. Just a dream. It was just pregnancy nerves. I wanted to believe that, but my mind kept racing. If the baby inherited my green hair…they’d almost certainly face discrimination because of it. The same way I had. While the most I ever had to deal with were neighborhood bullies, there was no guarantee that my child would be so fortunate. Something far, far worse could be waiting for them.

blocks.text: I knew Rudy would protect them whether they had green hair or not. Eris would do the same, and so would Roxy. My head told me they would, but my heart still worried.

blocks.text: It didn’t take long to realize why.
blocks.html: It didn’t take long to realize why.

blocks.text: I knew about the Laplace Factor. I knew why the color of my hair was green, and why Rudy had gotten a bit uneasy over the subject a while back.
blocks.html: I knew about the Laplace Factor. I knew why the color of my hair was green, and why Rudy had gotten a bit uneasy over the subject a while back.

blocks.text: What if the child I gave birth to turned out to be Laplace?
blocks.html: What if the child I gave birth to turned out to be Laplace?

blocks.text: I wondered, What would Rudy do? It wasn’t his priority now, but he was gathering forces to do battle with Laplace in eighty years. If my child really were Laplace, then, given what Rudy had done so far… Well, I couldn’t help but wonder.

blocks.text: I believed in Rudy. I wouldn’t doubt him for a second. But…what would he do? What would I want him to do? My mind spun over these thoughts for so long that I didn’t get another wink of sleep that night.

blocks.text: I comforted myself with the fact that there was no way to know if the child’s hair would be green. If their hair turned out to be any other color, we’d be fine.

scenes.location: Rudeus's house, Sharia (the nursery)

blocks.text: I NAMED THE BABY Sieghart. The names for my girls, Lucie and Lara, came from their mothers, while my son Arus was named after a famous hero in history. I decided to take inspiration from the invincible hero in my old world, Siegfried. I considered leaving it at just Siegfried, but Ranoa had a lot of names that went “[something]-hart,” so I tagged that on at the last minute.
blocks.html: I NAMED THE BABY Sieghart. The names for my girls, Lucie and Lara, came from their mothers, while my son Arus was named after a famous hero in history. I decided to take inspiration from the invincible hero in my old world, Siegfried. I considered leaving it at just Siegfried, but Ranoa had a lot of names that went “[something]-hart,” so I tagged that on at the last minute.

blocks.text: We’d call him “Sieg” for short.
blocks.html: We’d call him “Sieg” for short.

blocks.text: Sieg seemed like a perfectly normal child. He did all the crying, sleeping, peeing, and pooping you’d expect. Well, given that Lara barely cried at all and Arus would bawl the second I held him, Sieg seemed plenty normal in comparison.

blocks.text: As for being a reincarnation of a certain someone… Well, there’s no reason to be vague. I mean Laplace. And no, Sieg didn’t look like him.
blocks.html: As for being a reincarnation of a certain someone… Well, there’s no reason to be vague. I mean Laplace. And no, Sieg didn’t look like him.

blocks.text: “Not as far as I can tell, anyway,” I told myself. “Seriously, though. What’s going on with my kid?”

blocks.text: Three days had already passed since Arumanfi appeared and told me about the summons from Perugius. Right now, it was the middle of the night. Sitting across from me was Orsted. Between us lay Sieg, who snoozed peacefully in his cradle; he’d been crying until just a moment ago, but now he was fast asleep. Orsted seemed a bit tuckered out himself.

blocks.text: “Hmph. Did you not understand me the first time?”
blocks.html: “Hmph. Did you not understand me the first time?”

blocks.text: “Oh, no! Of course, I absolutely understand, and I believe you! Laplace hasn’t been born yet, so our child can’t be Laplace! Right, absolutely! I understand full well!”

blocks.text: “Pax’s death means that I no longer know where Laplace will be born…but the Laplace Factors have yet to be fully gathered. It could happen in about fifty years’ time, but Laplace wouldn’t be born now. Not under any circumstances.”

blocks.text: “So, what about the green hair?” I asked. Sieg’s hair was green. It was a similar shade to what Sylphie’s once was. The hair was still thin and fluffy on account of Sieg being a baby, but it was definitely green.

blocks.text: “This child is not Laplace,” Orsted continued. “That I can assure you.”

blocks.text: I thanked him, but I still had room for doubt. Orsted wasn’t infallible. It might not have happened in prior loops, but this loop had proven that there was a first time for everything. Orsted had made his share of miscalculations already. That was why I couldn’t shake the possibility of Perugius examining Sieg, concluding he was Laplace, and deciding to kill him on the spot. That, or the possibility of Perugius making a mistake.

blocks.text: “Okay…”
blocks.html: “Okay…”
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: No reaction was far from proof. Sylphie had hardly reacted, either.
blocks.html: No reaction was far from proof. Sylphie had hardly reacted, either.

blocks.text: Sylvaril continued walking without looking back at us. We passed through halls lined with luxurious decor until we found ourselves standing before a grand, tastefully designed door. Maybe seeing castles all around the world had changed my perspective… I was starting to understand why Zanoba had such glowing praise for this castle back then. Saying any of that out loud here would probably come off as brownnosing, though.

blocks.html: Sylvaril opened that grand door.

blocks.text: “Enter, if you’d please.”
blocks.html: “Enter, if you’d please.”
blocks.speaker: Sylvaril

blocks.text: At Sylvaril’s request, we entered the audience chamber. It was unchanged from when I saw it last. The pillars as wide as tree trunks, the giant chandeliers, the curtains emblazoned with the emblems of humanity and dragonfolk, and the twelve masked men and women standing on both sides of the red velvet carpet. Sitting on the throne was the silver-haired Dragon King.

Sitting on the throne was the silver-haired Dragon King.

blocks.text: The aesthetics of this place might be described as grand, glorious, or even divine. You could search the world over for an audience chamber that inspired half as much awe and never come close. The addition of Sylvaril would be the final piece in the puz—wait, was there someone extra here? Ah, Nanahoshi was mixed in. What was she doing here? Did she have a side gig as one of the spirit aides?

blocks.text: “Rudeus. You’ve arrived.”
blocks.html: “Rudeus. You’ve arrived.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “I have. It’s been some time, Lord Perugius.”
blocks.html: “I have. It’s been some time, Lord Perugius.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: I bowed my head but remained standing. Sylphie, Eris, and Zanoba all took a knee. I normally would have kneeled as well, but I’d recently learned that, as Orsted’s subordinate, I shouldn’t be so quick to kneel before others.

blocks.text: I checked their reactions to be sure; Sylvaril seemed a bit ticked off, but Perugius didn’t say anything about it. I couldn’t attribute this to his mood, however, which was foul.
blocks.html: I checked their reactions to be sure; Sylvaril seemed a bit ticked off, but Perugius didn’t say anything about it. I couldn’t attribute this to his mood, however, which was foul.

blocks.text: “You certainly kept me waiting.”
blocks.html: “You certainly kept me waiting.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “Well… My son had just been born.”
blocks.html: “Well… My son had just been born.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “I’ve heard as much from Arumanfi, hence my willingness to wait. I wouldn’t be so forgiving had your reason been any more trifling than that.”
blocks.html: “I’ve heard as much from Arumanfi, hence my willingness to wait. I wouldn’t be so forgiving had your reason been any more trifling than that.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: He might dismiss the birth of a child as “trifling,” but he wouldn’t castigate me over my choice. Truly a magnanimous monarch. He kept anxiously tapping on the dragon-shaped armrests of his throne.
blocks.html: He might dismiss the birth of a child as “trifling,” but he wouldn’t castigate me over my choice. Truly a magnanimous monarch. He kept anxiously tapping on the dragon-shaped armrests of his throne.

blocks.text: “I take it from the look on your face that you know why I called you here.”
blocks.html: “I take it from the look on your face that you know why I called you here.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “Yes, I do.”
blocks.html: “Yes, I do.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “And I take it from your party that you’re prepared to fight depending on how this conversation goes. Some commendable resolve.”
blocks.html: “And I take it from your party that you’re prepared to fight depending on how this conversation goes. Some commendable resolve.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “Yes… I am.”
blocks.html: “Yes… I am.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: Perugius glared bitterly at Orsted. I couldn’t see Orsted’s expression from beneath the black helmet, but I could guess that it was as intimidating as ever. Good ol’ reliable Orsted.
blocks.html: Perugius glared bitterly at Orsted. I couldn’t see Orsted’s expression from beneath the black helmet, but I could guess that it was as intimidating as ever. Good ol’ reliable Orsted.

blocks.text: “However, Lord Perugius, I believe it won’t come to that.”
blocks.html: “However, Lord Perugius, I believe it won’t come to that.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Well, now! It won’t lead to a fight, you say? I see, so you have that much confidence in your position!”
blocks.html: “Well, now! It won’t lead to a fight, you say? I see, so you have that much confidence in your position!”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “We don’t have any reason to fight. Now, then… Sylphie?”
blocks.html: “We don’t have any reason to fight. Now, then… Sylphie?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: I had Sylphie stand and show Perugius the baby she carried.
blocks.html: I had Sylphie stand and show Perugius the baby she carried.

blocks.text: “Lay your eyes upon my fourth child.”
blocks.html: “Lay your eyes upon my fourth child.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Hmm… Well? What of it?”
blocks.html: “Hmm… Well? What of it?”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “Well, everything. Were you not the one who requested I bring the child born between Sylphie and me, Lord Perugius?”
blocks.html: “Well, everything. Were you not the one who requested I bring the child born between Sylphie and me, Lord Perugius?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: Perugius stopped moving. His irritated tapping on the armrest stopped too. I continued regardless.
blocks.html: Perugius stopped moving. His irritated tapping on the armrest stopped too. I continued regardless.

blocks.text: “I had Orsted look at him as well, and we can confirm that this child is not Laplace. However, I presumed that you wouldn’t be satisfied unless you saw him with your own two eyes. I considered declining to show him to you, but to maintain our amicable relationship, I decided it best to allow it.”
blocks.html: “I had Orsted look at him as well, and we can confirm that this child is not Laplace. However, I presumed that you wouldn’t be satisfied unless you saw him with your own two eyes. I considered declining to show him to you, but to maintain our amicable relationship, I decided it best to allow it.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: Perugius remained silent.
blocks.html: Perugius remained silent.

blocks.text: “However, if Orsted was perhaps wrong, and if this child really is Laplace…”
blocks.html: “However, if Orsted was perhaps wrong, and if this child really is Laplace…”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Well? What then?”
blocks.html: “Well? What then?”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “Then I’ll fight.”
blocks.html: “Then I’ll fight.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: Perugius’s eyebrow twitched.
blocks.html: Perugius’s eyebrow twitched.

blocks.text: “Have you not been traveling the world for the sole purpose of defeating Laplace in battle eighty years from now?”
blocks.html: “Have you not been traveling the world for the sole purpose of defeating Laplace in battle eighty years from now?”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “I have.”
blocks.html: “I have.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Yet you would fight to defend that very same Laplace?”
blocks.html: “Yet you would fight to defend that very same Laplace?”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: Now that he mentioned it, I was contradicting myself. I would protect this child, despite knowing he was Laplace. It would completely waste everything I’d spend these past few years doing.
blocks.html: Now that he mentioned it, I was contradicting myself. I would protect this child, despite knowing he was Laplace. It would completely waste everything I’d spend these past few years doing.

blocks.text: “If my child grows up, and if he truly does bring about a war against all of humanity…then I’ll respond the way we’ve been preparing for all this time.”
blocks.html: “If my child grows up, and if he truly does bring about a war against all of humanity…then I’ll respond the way we’ve been preparing for all this time.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “You wouldn’t consider nipping this problem in the bud?”
blocks.html: “You wouldn’t consider nipping this problem in the bud?”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “I…would not.”
blocks.html: “I…would not.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: If my son were Laplace… A terrifying thought. I avoided thinking too deeply about it. In eighty years, Laplace would start a war. In response, I was negotiating with countries around the world to help ease Orsted’s burden. If Laplace were to appear right this moment, I’d probably fight in the war myself.
blocks.html: If my son were Laplace… A terrifying thought. I avoided thinking too deeply about it. In eighty years, Laplace would start a war. In response, I was negotiating with countries around the world to help ease Orsted’s burden. If Laplace were to appear right this moment, I’d probably fight in the war myself.

blocks.text: Stop for a moment and think it through. If a war never broke out, what then? If Laplace were to regain his senses and swear off of war, what then? Let’s say Laplace had just been born; there should be plenty of time to make him see reason. His schooling could make a difference. If we taught Laplace about everything that happened and everything that would come to pass, he might even become Orsted’s ally…

Let’s say Laplace had just been born; there should be plenty of time to make him see reason. His schooling could make a difference. If we taught Laplace about everything that happened and everything that would come to pass, he might even become Orsted’s ally…

blocks.text: No. Orsted was clear; Laplace had to be killed. He must obtain the treasure of the dragonfolk. Which meant that the day would come where Orsted took my child’s life… Damn. No other conclusion.
blocks.html: No. Orsted was clear; Laplace had to be killed. He must obtain the treasure of the dragonfolk. Which meant that the day would come where Orsted took my child’s life… Damn. No other conclusion.

blocks.text: Hold on, Rudeus. Caaalm down. If I took each thought one step at a time, I could find the path I wanted to take.
blocks.html: Hold on, Rudeus. Caaalm down. If I took each thought one step at a time, I could find the path I wanted to take.

blocks.text: “My family will always come first in my priorities. I became a subordinate of Orsted’s because there were forces at work to harm them. If Orsted were planning to harm my family, then he’d have to do so over my dead body.”
blocks.html: “My family will always come first in my priorities. I became a subordinate of Orsted’s because there were forces at work to harm them. If Orsted were planning to harm my family, then he’d have to do so over my dead body.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Even if the cause were your own son?”
blocks.html: “Even if the cause were your own son?”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “My plan…is to thoroughly teach him the difference between right and wrong. My children may be young, but while they’re still children—that is, until they turn fifteen—I will protect them. If they were to turn away from my advice after that, then I’d own up to my responsibility and deal with them.”
blocks.html: “My plan…is to thoroughly teach him the difference between right and wrong. My children may be young, but while they’re still children—that is, until they turn fifteen—I will protect them. If they were to turn away from my advice after that, then I’d own up to my responsibility and deal with them.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Well, now. ‘Deal with them,’ you say. Might I ask how?”
blocks.html: “Well, now. ‘Deal with them,’ you say. Might I ask how?”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “I’ll…teach them again. As best as I can.”
blocks.html: “I’ll…teach them again. As best as I can.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: As best as I could. For what I couldn’t, well, being a child would be no excuse… Or, wait…
blocks.html: As best as I could. For what I couldn’t, well, being a child would be no excuse… Or, wait…

blocks.text: “So… You won’t say you’d kill them.”
blocks.html: “So… You won’t say you’d kill them.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Everyone makes mistakes, so I’d like to give my children a second chance.”
blocks.html: “Everyone makes mistakes, so I’d like to give my children a second chance.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: That was the most I could say. I didn’t want to put anything beyond that into words. I didn’t want to think about a future in which Lucie, Lara, or Arus made enemies of Orsted and were ruthlessly killed.
blocks.html: That was the most I could say. I didn’t want to put anything beyond that into words. I didn’t want to think about a future in which Lucie, Lara, or Arus made enemies of Orsted and were ruthlessly killed.

blocks.text: But however lofty my lessons might be, there were times when that just wouldn’t be enough. Children rarely grow the way their parents plan. Heck, my own life barely went the way I planned it. They might have been my children, but I couldn’t expect them to live up to every hope I had for them. They were their own people. That’s why I wanted to give them a chance, if nothing else. A compromise.

blocks.text: “I have no children. As such, I fail to understand these ideas of yours. Ideas of allowing the seed of misfortune to grow only to weed it out yourself.” Perugius laughed at his observation.
blocks.html: “I have no children. As such, I fail to understand these ideas of yours. Ideas of allowing the seed of misfortune to grow only to weed it out yourself.” Perugius laughed at his observation.
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “But you, you’re a foolish enough man to pick a fight with death for the sake of protecting your wives. Of course I wouldn’t understand. I can’t understand…but I can tell how strong your conviction is.”
blocks.html: “But you, you’re a foolish enough man to pick a fight with death for the sake of protecting your wives. Of course I wouldn’t understand. I can’t understand…but I can tell how strong your conviction is.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: Perugius descended from his throne and slowly walked toward us. He soon stood right in front of me, with his height demanding that I tilt my head upward.
blocks.html: Perugius descended from his throne and slowly walked toward us. He soon stood right in front of me, with his height demanding that I tilt my head upward.

blocks.text: “In light of this, I shall grant you a chance and a trial.”
blocks.html: “In light of this, I shall grant you a chance and a trial.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “What do you mean?”
blocks.html: “What do you mean?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Take your baby and travel to the shrine upon Aluce Hill, so that he may be baptized.”
blocks.html: “Take your baby and travel to the shrine upon Aluce Hill, so that he may be baptized.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “Aluce Hill?”
blocks.html: “Aluce Hill?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: It was a landmark I’d never heard of. I looked around; almost everyone was tilting their heads in befuddlement. Orsted wasn’t, but I couldn’t make out his expression from under the helmet, either. Not that I thought that name was news to him, of course.
blocks.html: It was a landmark I’d never heard of. I looked around; almost everyone was tilting their heads in befuddlement. Orsted wasn’t, but I couldn’t make out his expression from under the helmet, either. Not that I thought that name was news to him, of course.

blocks.text: “Will that do, Nanahoshi?” asked Perugius while I was still processing the previous command. Curious as to why Nanahoshi’s name would come up here, I looked her way.
blocks.html: “Will that do, Nanahoshi?” asked Perugius while I was still processing the previous command. Curious as to why Nanahoshi’s name would come up here, I looked her way.
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “I still haven’t wrapped my head around all of this…but I owe Rudeus a lot, so I’ll be fine.”
blocks.html: “I still haven’t wrapped my head around all of this…but I owe Rudeus a lot, so I’ll be fine.”
blocks.speaker: Nanahoshi

blocks.text: Nanahoshi sighed as she responded, like she was kinda let down. Maybe she had some other business here? She would need a good reason to stand among the familiars.
blocks.html: Nanahoshi sighed as she responded, like she was kinda let down. Maybe she had some other business here? She would need a good reason to stand among the familiars.

blocks.text: Sorry, but I had to steal the spotlight here. Family came first.
blocks.html: Sorry, but I had to steal the spotlight here. Family came first.

blocks.text: “Lord Perugius, where is this Aluce Hill?”
blocks.html: “Lord Perugius, where is this Aluce Hill?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Look for it yourself…is what I’d like to say, but I shall tell you. It’s hardly worth keeping secret when Orsted surely knows.”
blocks.html: “Look for it yourself…is what I’d like to say, but I shall tell you. It’s hardly worth keeping secret when Orsted surely knows.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

blocks.text: “Ah, right. My apologies, but I appreciate the effort.”
blocks.html: “Ah, right. My apologies, but I appreciate the effort.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: In a clear, booming voice, he uttered the name of the one continent I had yet to set foot on.
blocks.html: In a clear, booming voice, he uttered the name of the one continent I had yet to set foot on.

blocks.text: “The Divine Continent.”
blocks.html: “The Divine Continent.”
blocks.speaker: Perugius

scenes.location: Orsted Corporation office, Sharia

blocks.text: THE DIVINE CONTINENT.
blocks.html: THE DIVINE CONTINENT.

blocks.text: If you were to mark it on a map, it’d be on the northernmost edge, connecting the Central Continent to the Demon Continent. While it is called a continent, its land is adjoined to the Central Continent. You could even walk from it to the Demon Continent during the low tide.
blocks.html: If you were to mark it on a map, it’d be on the northernmost edge, connecting the Central Continent to the Demon Continent. While it is called a continent, its land is adjoined to the Central Continent. You could even walk from it to the Demon Continent during the low tide.

blocks.text: Why would this landmass be treated as separate from both the Central and Demon Continents? Its height. This continent perched atop a steep, vertical precipice about three thousand meters above sea level.
blocks.html: Why would this landmass be treated as separate from both the Central and Demon Continents? Its height. This continent perched atop a steep, vertical precipice about three thousand meters above sea level.

blocks.text: People did not travel through it as a rule. It wasn’t impossible for those determined enough, but there were no roads worth mentioning. Given the winged monsters teeming within the walls of that cliff, any attempts at scaling it would be incredibly difficult. I’d heard stories about wanted fugitives from the Central Continent traveling through the Divine Continent in the hopes of reaching the Demon Continent and escaping their bounty hunters. I hadn’t heard any stories about them surviving the attempt.

blocks.text: You’d think being able to fly would make being a fugitive easy, but in this world, the sky belonged to the dragons. Forget planes; this world’s technology hadn’t even developed hot air balloons. It was the height of recklessness for someone to go into the air unprotected.

blocks.text: And this was the place Perugius wanted me to bring a month-old baby? Absurd.
blocks.html: And this was the place Perugius wanted me to bring a month-old baby? Absurd.

blocks.text: “I’d appreciate it if you could inform me of where I could find a teleportation circle linked to this Divine Continent.”
blocks.html: “I’d appreciate it if you could inform me of where I could find a teleportation circle linked to this Divine Continent.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: We were back at my company’s countryside office. Eris was right behind me. Roxy and Sylphie were with Sieg in a different room. It didn’t seem like we’d be fighting Perugius at the moment, so I had Zanoba return home.

blocks.text: Orsted’s expression was as fearsome as ever, but behind that fearsome face, he seemed to be considering how to tell me a hard truth. Maybe there wasn’t a teleportation circle connected to the Divine Continent?
blocks.html: Orsted’s expression was as fearsome as ever, but behind that fearsome face, he seemed to be considering how to tell me a hard truth. Maybe there wasn’t a teleportation circle connected to the Divine Continent?

blocks.text: “Perugius wouldn’t be satisfied if you used a teleportation circle.”
blocks.html: “Perugius wouldn’t be satisfied if you used a teleportation circle.”
blocks.speaker: Orsted

blocks.text: “Oh, that makes sense.”
blocks.html: “Oh, that makes sense.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: Come to think of it, Perugius did call it a “trial.” Perhaps giving Sieg a baptism at Aluce Hill on the Divine Continent wasn’t the only part of the trial; the perilous path toward reaching it might be important. If that meant going from here all the way to the Divine Continent on foot, we’d be wasting a lot of time.

blocks.text: “Does that rule out teleporting to somewhere near the Divine Continent?”
blocks.html: “Does that rule out teleporting to somewhere near the Divine Continent?”

blocks.text: “It shouldn’t be a problem if you’re still outside of it.”
blocks.html: “It shouldn’t be a problem if you’re still outside of it.”
blocks.speaker: Orsted

blocks.text: So, bring the baby to the foot of the Divine Continent, do some rock climbing, and get him baptized by the people living at the top. A three-course meal of tribulations. Forget the difficulty of the trek by itself, this was a one-month-old baby we’d be traveling with. He could get sick at any point along the way. At three thousand feet above sea level, altitude sickness could be a real possibility…

blocks.text: Yeah, this would be rough. Guess that’s what made it a trial, though.

blocks.text: “Hmm…”
blocks.html: “Hmm…”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: You know, maybe bringing the floating fortress crashing down wasn’t such a bad idea.

blocks.text: “Orsted, do you think I can complete this trial? With a one-month-old baby with me, that is.”

blocks.text: “Sure.”
blocks.html: “Sure.”

blocks.text: “Your reasoning?”
blocks.html: “Your reasoning?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Sieghart, was it? That baby’s physique shows strong influence from the Laplace Factor. Children like that have a resistance to typical illnesses and environmental stresses.”
blocks.html: “Sieghart, was it? That baby’s physique shows strong influence from the Laplace Factor. Children like that have a resistance to typical illnesses and environmental stresses.”
blocks.speaker: Orsted

blocks.text: “Oh, I see.”
blocks.html: “Oh, I see.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “It’s an effect they wove into the reincarnation magic to make sure that Laplace’s future body would survive the harshest conditions. If a child has a strong Factor, they can survive the trip to the Divine Continent.”
blocks.html: “It’s an effect they wove into the reincarnation magic to make sure that Laplace’s future body would survive the harshest conditions. If a child has a strong Factor, they can survive the trip to the Divine Continent.”

blocks.text: All right. If Orsted was that confident, then I guess Sieg would be fine. You know, as long as I didn’t totally space out and let a roc swipe Sieg off my back and carry him away in its talons. Eris and Roxy should be coming with me, so they’d make up for any lapses in attention I could have.

blocks.text: “I understand.”

blocks.text: “I appreciate the generosity…”

blocks.text: “I still remember how you wiped a forest off the face of the continent to protect your family. I wouldn’t put it past you to bring Chaos Breaker crashing down before Laplace’s revival. That’s an asset, and I will need it.”

blocks.text: Figures. To Orsted, both Perugius and I were combat assets. He didn’t want his pieces taking one another out.

blocks.text: “Is that all right with you, Eris?”

blocks.text: “Makes no difference to me,” said Eris. She then shot me a look that I hadn’t seen much of lately: a piercing glare. “Don’t you think you should discuss it with Sylphie?”

blocks.text: I WAS AT A LOSS. I didn’t know who to ask what to do or how. I didn’t even know what I wanted to come of it. It was painful to be so clueless.
blocks.html: I WAS AT A LOSS. I didn’t know who to ask what to do or how. I didn’t even know what I wanted to come of it. It was painful to be so clueless.

blocks.text: When Rudy told me that he’d show Sieg to Perugius, I thought for just a moment about how much easier it would be if Perugius would simply take Sieg away. The thought shook me to my core.
blocks.html: When Rudy told me that he’d show Sieg to Perugius, I thought for just a moment about how much easier it would be if Perugius would simply take Sieg away. The thought shook me to my core.

blocks.text: It was just a fleeting thought, but it confirmed something—the root of my anxieties wasn’t the idea of Sieg being Laplace. But that begged the question: What was it I feared? Why was I uneasy? I didn’t know. All I could do was hold Sieg in my arms and shudder.

blocks.text: Even when we were told to go to the Divine Continent and give him a baptism, my mind was blank. It really was like I’d reverted to my old self—to the little girl who was bullied by all the kids in Buena Village. Rudy saved me back then; he chased off the bullies and taught me all there was to know. Things like magic, and how to read and write. What about now? Would Rudy still save me?

blocks.text: When I was a foolish little child, I had complete faith in Rudy and knew he would save me. Things were different now. I loved Rudy, and I had faith in him. But I knew he was still only human. He might have looked infallible, like he could do anything, but the truth was plenty of things were beyond him. He was scared of all kinds of things, of course, and he was more than capable of making simple mistakes.

blocks.text: Like forgetting to come up with a name for our baby. That surprised me, and even disappointed me, but it wasn’t like I got angry over it. Rudy was hard at work as Orsted’s subordinate. I knew how busy every single day was for him. I knew that he faced hardship in the Asura Kingdom, in Millis, on the Demon Continent. Everywhere he went.

blocks.text: People had their limits. I wanted to be considerate of that. I couldn’t expect someone to be a perfect family man while working under Orsted. That was why I swore to myself that I’d do it, so that Rudy could be free to pursue his work. I mustn’t beg Rudy for help. I had to make ends meet on my own.

blocks.text: “Sylphie.”
blocks.html: “Sylphie.”
blocks.speaker: Roxy

blocks.text: While my head spun from the onslaught of questions that had no answer, I heard a voice. I was instantly snapped back to reality, catching the person who’d spoken my name in the corner of my eye.

blocks.text: It was Roxy.
blocks.html: It was Roxy.

blocks.text: “Um… Sorry if I’ve got the wrong idea,” Roxy began, asking with both hesitation and sincerity. “But… Sylphie, do you think that maybe you’re less concerned about whether Sieg is Laplace, and more worried about how his hair is green?”

blocks.text: By the time I realized it, my eyes met Roxy’s. Mine must have widened.
blocks.html: By the time I realized it, my eyes met Roxy’s. Mine must have widened.

blocks.text: “What…makes you say that?”
blocks.html: “What…makes you say that?”
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: “I heard from Lilia that you used to be bullied by other children for having green hair.”
blocks.html: “I heard from Lilia that you used to be bullied by other children for having green hair.”
blocks.speaker: Roxy

blocks.text: Oh, right. Lilia! I wondered why I’d forgotten about her. A long time had passed since my hair changed colors; I reunited with Rudy, married him, and at some point, I’d started assuming Rudy was the only one around who still knew about the old me. Silly me, Lilia knew as well. I never gave it too much thought, but there was no way she wouldn’t have known.

blocks.text: Why didn’t I ever connect with her? No, Lilia did start conversations with me. I had just closed myself off and never tried to ask her.

blocks.text: “You probably don’t remember, Sylphie, but back when I was in Buena Village, I met you once. I even spoke to your parents.”

blocks.text: “About…what?”
blocks.html: “About…what?”
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: “About the color of your hair. It seemed they worried about it, too.”
blocks.html: “About the color of your hair. It seemed they worried about it, too.”
blocks.speaker: Roxy

blocks.text: Huh. This was, well, a strange thing to hear.
blocks.html: Huh. This was, well, a strange thing to hear.

blocks.text: For as long as I could remember, my mother and father never said a word about my hair color. Even when I got bullied and ran home crying and asked them why my hair was a different color from everyone else’s, they couldn’t give me a straight answer; they just looked sad, or guilty, or some other mix of emotions, and then they hugged me and told me it was all right, but it wasn’t all right at all—

blocks.text: “What did you tell them?”
blocks.html: “What did you tell them?”
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: “That I could guarantee you weren’t a Superd. I told them that everything would be all right if they explained it to their neighbors and raised you with love.”
blocks.html: “That I could guarantee you weren’t a Superd. I told them that everything would be all right if they explained it to their neighbors and raised you with love.”
blocks.speaker: Roxy

blocks.text: Ah. So that was why my mother and father hugged me and told me that it was all right, over and over again.
blocks.html: Ah. So that was why my mother and father hugged me and told me that it was all right, over and over again.

blocks.text: Of course, they weren’t all talk; I knew that my mother and father really did love me. They raised me as best they could. I might not have known it then, but I knew now.

blocks.text: “I thought you’d be all right since Buena Village didn’t have a culture of discriminating against demons, but that attitude doesn’t always reach the children…”
blocks.html: “I thought you’d be all right since Buena Village didn’t have a culture of discriminating against demons, but that attitude doesn’t always reach the children…”
blocks.speaker: Roxy

blocks.text: Roxy paused to pat my chest.
blocks.html: Roxy paused to pat my chest.

blocks.text: “Either way, if you have any concern about Sieg being treated differently because of his hair color, just leave it to me. As you can see from looking at me, I’m very clearly a demon. I’ve got plenty of experience with handling discrimination!”

blocks.text: Still… Yeah, she was right. I wasn’t alone anymore. I had Lilia and Roxy. Raising children might not have been Eris’s specialty, but she gave it her all without giving up or pushing it on to someone else.

blocks.text: “Let’s all travel to the Divine Continent together. I’m a bit concerned about leaving Lilia alone to watch the house, but there are plenty of people she can rely on.”

Roxy looked even more determined than usual, so I wondered if she gave Sylphie a pep talk. Man, Roxy was reliable.

blocks.text: On the first day, we confirmed our route and schedule with Orsted, learned about the peculiarities of the Divine Continent, put in our orders for equipment, and a few other things. Fortunately, the office was already connected to a series of ancient teleportation circles around the world.

blocks.text: Our plan for the first day was to travel to an ancient circle from the office, soar from the ancient circle to the foot of the Divine Continent, and then scale the cliff face. Once that was cleared, traveling for around a half day to a full day would land us in Aluce.

blocks.text: Aluce was the name of a skyfolk town, with Aluce Hill referring to a hill nearby. After staying a night in the town, we would climb the nearby Aluce Hill and have Sieg receive his baptism. After that, all we’d have to do is set up a teleportation circle somewhere and head home.

blocks.text: Since we’d be climbing to a high altitude, we might need safety gear. The human body wasn’t well adapted to survival in low-oxygen areas. After I brought it up with Orsted, he provided a solution immediately.

blocks.text: Orsted handed me a few necklace-shaped magical implements. Apparently, they’d nullify the harmful effects of thin air. They were originally invented by a race that traversed the miasma-filled valleys of the Demon Continent, so their primary effect was to nullify bodily harm that came from highly toxic areas. It seemed like they’d work for our climb to the Divine Continent as well.

blocks.text: She hadn’t been getting much attention lately, given Sylphie’s emotional state. I guess this was only natural. I felt guilty over making a child pay the price for her parents’ problems, but parents were human too. We get depressed sometimes.

I couldn’t tell her to be a big sister and suck it up at her age, and I certainly didn’t want to, but I explained that the other kids would have tough times of their own. I hoped I could count on Lucie’s help when those times came. I also said that if she ever needed help, her dear ol’ dad would do everything he could to provide it.

She’d taken my words to heart.

blocks.text: A few hours after our departure, we arrived at the Divine Continent’s border. We were on the furthest northeastern edge of the Central Continent.
blocks.html: A few hours after our departure, we arrived at the Divine Continent’s border. We were on the furthest northeastern edge of the Central Continent.

blocks.text: A vertical precipice that we strained to see the top of towered in front and over us. On either side, the ocean stretched into the distance.
blocks.html: A vertical precipice that we strained to see the top of towered in front and over us. On either side, the ocean stretched into the distance.

blocks.text: The cliff face was more than simple bare rock. A number of the local inhabitants believed that gods resided within this cliff, so its surface was dotted with ladders and footholds. According to Orsted, a shrine dedicated to the worship of these gods could be found around two hundred meters up.

It was patchy, but it continued all the way to the Demon Continent. While it was no doubt a harrowing path, it was apparently a safer bet than trying to climb upward. Quite a few people had traversed it from here to the Demon Continent and vice versa.

blocks.text: Her voice seemed to plead for me to have a plan. Which, of course, I did. Come now, would I really go rock climbing with a newborn baby without a plan?
blocks.html: Her voice seemed to plead for me to have a plan. Which, of course, I did. Come now, would I really go rock climbing with a newborn baby without a plan?

blocks.text: “This way, everyone,” I said, leading the group toward a part of the wall that was relatively bare of footholds. Not that the presence of footholds would make a difference, but I didn’t want to make life harder for any travelers coming after me.
blocks.html: “This way, everyone,” I said, leading the group toward a part of the wall that was relatively bare of footholds. Not that the presence of footholds would make a difference, but I didn’t want to make life harder for any travelers coming after me.
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: First, I used earth magic to create a box that could hold about four adults with plenty of breathing space. One that was heavy but sturdy. I then added an entrance, as well as some windows to let some light in and let us check our surroundings.

blocks.text: “All aboard.”
blocks.html: “All aboard.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: Once I confirmed that everyone was inside, I closed the door.
blocks.html: Once I confirmed that everyone was inside, I closed the door.

blocks.text: “The heck is this?” asked Eris, who tilted her head and looked at me out of the corner of her eye.
blocks.html: “The heck is this?” asked Eris, who tilted her head and looked at me out of the corner of her eye.
blocks.speaker: Eris

blocks.text: “Now, now, let the master do his work,” I assured her. I placed a hand on the ground. The spell I’d readied was called Stone Pillar. I formed four pillars, fixed them firmly to the box, and pumped in some mana.

blocks.text: “Eep!”

blocks.text: The box slowly started moving. Upward.
blocks.html: The box slowly started moving. Upward.

blocks.text: “Oh! Well, this does seem like a safe way to do it.”
blocks.html: “Oh! Well, this does seem like a safe way to do it.”

blocks.text: I felt a smug grin coming on at Roxy’s praise. This was an original spell of mine, Elevator. I used it once before, back on the Begaritt Continent.

blocks.text: I’d put even more thought into passenger safety since then. The pillars lifting the box up were kept sturdy with plenty of mana, ensuring they wouldn’t break on us. Creating pillars that could withstand the trip to three thousand meters required a massive amount of mana, so I did a baton pass every fifty meters by creating new pillars. I figured we’d be fine, but in case I got tired or ran low on mana on the way up, I could also make a hole in the cliff face and slot the entire box inside it, giving me a way to safely take a breather.

blocks.text: Sylphie glanced out the window while holding Sieg; a moment later, her face went completely pale. She walked over to me and plopped down by my side. Given how complicated things had gotten in the past few weeks, it warmed my heart to see she still relied on me.

blocks.text: “Man… Talk about boring,” said Eris, who had also sat down—but only because she’d grown bored of the view out the window.

blocks.text: “Hmph!”

blocks.text: Eris turned up her nose. I took the fact that she didn’t hit me as a sign that she completely understood. I wouldn’t let myself hurt those two on this journey. Not a scratch. No amount of heroism was gonna make up for forgetting to name Sieg, though.

blocks.text: Several hours passed. My plan of swapping out the pillars every fifty meters was making our ascent go without a hitch.
blocks.html: Several hours passed. My plan of swapping out the pillars every fifty meters was making our ascent go without a hitch.

blocks.text: Sylphie kept her eyes on Sieg the whole time. Roxy tried to lighten the mood with a little light conversation. Sylphie wasn’t her usual self, but she managed to respond. It was small talk; Roxy’s grumblings about her work, the latest happenings at school, the last prank Lucie pulled on her, asking about how Arus and Lara were doing. That sort of thing. I would’ve liked to join in, but those pillars weren’t exactly gonna form themselves, so I was stuck with that.

blocks.text: As for Eris, she took position by the window and gazed outside. The scenery was lovely. As the ground steadily slipped away, we got a better view of the flocks of giant creatures flying between the gaps of the clouds. Were those Blue Dragons? I’d never seen Blue Dragons up close…

blocks.text: By the time I replaced the pillars for the twentieth time and put us above the thousand-meter mark, avian monsters started to come into view. They were giant birds—probably around three meters long, with a wingspan exceeding six meters. They were also flying around our box and squawking at us. Their flock circled us, perched above us, pecked at the walls. Generally harassed us. Hard to tell if they were scared of this new object, or territorial and trying to destroy it.

blocks.text: Our box was built to be incredibly tough. It wouldn’t break from a few monsters’ pokes. It did sway a little, though. Each time it did, the color drained from Sylphie’s face, Sieg would start crying, and Roxy would reassure them that everything was fine and that we wouldn’t fall. Not that Roxy knew enough to make that promise.

blocks.text: I knew we wouldn’t fall. If I ever thought we might, I’d have fixed the box to the cliff face and exterminated those monsters. With no reason to think they were a threat, I continued our ascent. The monsters managed to jam their necks through the window every now and then, but Eris would quickly lop them off, and that was the end of that. The soil of the box started to become stained with their blood, but hey, it wasn’t like we’d spent all our lives in the lap of luxury, you know? We weren’t sheltered and could all stand a bit of gore. Nobody complained.

blocks.text: After a while, I slotted the box into the cliff face, rinsed the walls off with a bit of water, and took a break. My somewhat late lunch came in a box that Lilia and Aisha had prepared as we departed. It was a sandwich. Two hardened slices of bread with some meat and vegetables stuck in the middle. It had a simple taste to it, not far off from my usual fare, but having a bite while looking over the vast scenery outside wasn’t half bad.

blocks.text: “Hey widdle Sieg, it’s Daddyyy. Time to get you in the bath, champ!”

blocks.text: I was looking after Sieg while Sylphie ate. I changed his diaper and then made a little tub with earth magic to bathe him in.
blocks.html: I was looking after Sieg while Sylphie ate. I changed his diaper and then made a little tub with earth magic to bathe him in.

blocks.text: This close, his hair really was green, and his ears were maybe just a bit longer than a human’s. His face was the perfect average of mine and Sylphie’s. Naturally. I would’ve been worried if he didn’t have any of my features.

blocks.text: He laughed when I brought my face in close and played peekaboo, and stared off into space when I moved away. When I picked him up, he’d stare deep into my face.
blocks.html: He laughed when I brought my face in close and played peekaboo, and stared off into space when I moved away. When I picked him up, he’d stare deep into my face.

blocks.text: When Lucie was born, she looked incredulous at every movement she made, which made me worry that she might have been a reincarnation. I was on my fourth child now, so I’d stopped having those sorts of doubts. No matter how many children I had, I knew I’d love all of them.

blocks.text: When I offered my index finger to Sieg, he gripped it tight. He was pretty strong. Babies are born pretty strong, huh?

blocks.text: I heard a snap accompanied by a sudden rush of pain. My instincts told me to yank my hand away from Sieg, but I took a breath, and then calmly used my left hand to peel Sieg’s hand off of my finger.

blocks.text: “Sieg?” shouted Sylphie as she sprang over in the next instant. When she saw my finger, her eyes widened. “Huh? Rudy, your finger…”

blocks.text: Sylphie was at a loss for words. Eventually, she lifted her hands to mine and wrapped them around my index finger. A faint light glowed from within her cupped hands and the pain disappeared.

blocks.text: He might even set out to slay a hydra or something… Wait, did his dad die in that story? I’d be another Paul.

blocks.text: Despite Zanoba being a little wild when he was young, he grew up to have a perfectly healthy obsession with dolls. That’s probably what Sylphie was referring to. She might not have known, however, that he was a capable man on the battlefield. In raw force, sure, but also in courage and cunning.

I couldn’t deny that Norn and the other University of Magic students were learning plenty about swordsmanship from her. I wouldn’t refer to the things she taught as “classes,” but from what I heard, the expertise she passed on was valuable.

blocks.text: We resumed our long ascent.
blocks.html: We resumed our long ascent.

blocks.text: We stopped seeing the avian monsters at around two thousand meters. In their place, we saw monsters that looked like winged goats and snake-necked lizards. The lizards lived in the crevices of the cliff face. They popped their heads in through the window that faced the cliff and startled us all. Their long necks allowed them to maneuver their heads with an alarming precision, and they were coming for us. Or they would have been, had we not separated their heads from their bodies in five seconds flat.

blocks.text: They must have evolved necks like that to drag prey into the crevices of the precipice. Excluding those guys, our trip was uneventful. We bagged one of the goats for dinner and ignored the rest as we continued our climb.

blocks.text: I had now swapped the pillars over sixty times.
blocks.html: I had now swapped the pillars over sixty times.

blocks.text: The world outside was blanketed in a thick fog. We had to be poking into the clouds by now.
blocks.html: The world outside was blanketed in a thick fog. We had to be poking into the clouds by now.

blocks.text: It was already night. Our box was illuminated by my lamplight spirit, but I was fatigued, and conflicted as to whether I should stop for a nap or if I should continue climbing. Given our elevation, we should be close to our destination…

blocks.text: As that thought crossed my mind, the fog happened to clear, and with it, the view outside the window. Not just the one facing away from the precipice, but the one facing toward it, as well.

blocks.text: I stopped raising the pillars. Outside, a grassy field shimmered in the moonlight.

chapters.title: Aluce, City of the Divine Continent

scenes.location: A campsite on the Divine Continent plain

blocks.text: SO THERE we were.
blocks.html: SO THERE we were.

blocks.text: As we got our bearings after stepping out of the box, a wide, open plain spread out before us. Maybe it was the cold, or maybe it was the thin air, but there wasn’t so much as a single tree growing. The ground was covered in nothing but short grass and shrubbery.
blocks.html: As we got our bearings after stepping out of the box, a wide, open plain spread out before us. Maybe it was the cold, or maybe it was the thin air, but there wasn’t so much as a single tree growing. The ground was covered in nothing but short grass and shrubbery.

blocks.text: Well, we were three thousand meters above sea level. Our breaths turned white in the chill. Fortunately, there wasn’t any snow, and the land was smooth and flat. It wouldn’t be too hard to travel. It was looking like we’d make good time and reach Aluce within a day.

blocks.text: For now, though, the moon was high in the sky. The stars twinkled brightly down upon us, possibly because we were that much closer to them. The night hid plenty of monsters, and it was easy to get lost in the dark.

blocks.text: For now, we set up camp.
blocks.html: For now, we set up camp.

blocks.text: We decided to eat the goats we’d hunted earlier. We made a campfire, heated up some water in a pot I made with earth magic, and tossed in some goat bones to make the stock. We added the meat once the water was boiling as well as some spices we brought along. Voilà, goat soup.

blocks.text: It was Geese who taught me how to cook monsters like this. Now he was my enemy. You never know where life might take you.
blocks.html: It was Geese who taught me how to cook monsters like this. Now he was my enemy. You never know where life might take you.

blocks.text: Anyway, it was cold out, so I moved the box onto the continent’s shelf. We’d all huddle together and sleep inside of it. There wasn’t any firewood lying around, but I’d brought a night’s worth of our own stock just in case. We moved the campfire into the box, crafted a chimney in the roof, and slept in a warmed room.

blocks.text: The adults here had done enough traveling to not mind a little cold, but we had to consider Sylphie’s body and Sieg. Sieg’s cheeks were bright red, but it didn’t seem like he had a fever. He was doing fine. Just as Orsted’d said, his body was built tough. Still, infants could easily get sick, so I had to keep an eye out.

blocks.text: Snuggling up with the ladies caused my little lad (the one not named Sieg or Arus) to spring wide awake, but I controlled myself. Sorry, Sieg, a new baby brother or sister will have to wait a while.

scenes.location: The Divine Continent plain, on the road to Aluce

blocks.text: The next day, we trekked onward.
blocks.html: The next day, we trekked onward.

blocks.text: The city of Aluce was northeast of our current location, with nothing but wide, empty plains in between. It didn’t look like there was a landmark in sight…at first.
blocks.html: The city of Aluce was northeast of our current location, with nothing but wide, empty plains in between. It didn’t look like there was a landmark in sight…at first.

blocks.text: Long ago, a hero came to this land and crossed the Divine Continent. In the era of the Laplace War, he climbed to the Divine Continent from the Demon Continent side, and then obtained a hidden skill that would prove invaluable to their victory. In case he met with an untimely demise, the hero left landmarks showing the path toward the technique he obtained.

In case he met with an untimely demise, the hero left landmarks showing the path toward the technique he obtained.

blocks.text: Incidentally, that hero went by the name of “Perugius.”
blocks.html: Incidentally, that hero went by the name of “Perugius.”

blocks.text: Given that the land here had short grass and few trees, the markers stood out pretty blatantly. All we had to do was glance around once morning came, and what do you know? One was right over there.
blocks.html: Given that the land here had short grass and few trees, the markers stood out pretty blatantly. All we had to do was glance around once morning came, and what do you know? One was right over there.

blocks.text: As we approached, we found that the landmarks were pillars. They were about a meter and a half tall, likely made from earth magic. They were just thick enough for you to wrap your arms around. The upper part of the pillar was scuffed and worn down by time. If you took a cross section, you could see that the pillar wasn’t cylindrical, but instead shaped like a drop. The tapered tip of that drop pointed toward the city.

blocks.text: So it was written in The Legend of Perugius. This landmark doubtless only made sense to the people who read that book. As I’d expect from a trial given by Perugius himself, his book held plenty of hints. Not that I thought he wrote the thing himself.

blocks.text: A few hours passed as we traveled.
blocks.html: A few hours passed as we traveled.

blocks.text: Maybe it was because we were on a plain and not a highway, but there were a lot of monsters around. They mostly fell into one of three types: the Winged Goats that first appeared at around two thousand meters up, the Heaven’s Mustelas that looked like four-meter-long weasels, and the giant, bipedal birds of prey known as Nidhogg Ostriches. There didn’t seem to be many amphibian or insect monsters, assumedly because it was cold all year round up here. In terms of strength, I’d put them on the same level as the monsters in the northern part of the Central Continent. They weren’t as weak as those found near Asura Kingdom or Millis, but they also weren’t as strong as those on the Demon Continent or the Begaritt Continent. The only monsters that made flocks numbering in the double digits were the Winged Goats, with the Heaven’s Mustelas and Nidhogg Ostriches roaming either alone or in the occasional pair.

blocks.text: I’d put the Winged Goats at D rank, and the other two in the C range. They were all capable of flight, however, so I’d have to bump them up a rank if they appeared in the Central Continent. People have a psychological weakness against things that can fly.

blocks.text: For adventurers like us, it goes without saying they posed almost no threat. Eris diverted the Winged Goats’ attention while Roxy hung back to launch a high-rank spell to wipe them out. Eris could finish the other two kinds by herself without thinking about it. They couldn’t reach me, much less Sieg or Sylphie. Ah, I was so grateful to the man of the house for protecting us!

blocks.text: The Divine Continent labyrinth known as Hell housed hordes of the world’s nastiest monsters, with its innermost sanctum guarded by a vicious slime called Vita. The mention of a slime reminded me of the Demon King one back in the Library Labyrinth. According to Orsted, this one was on another level. We didn’t want to go near it.

blocks.text: I wasn’t going to breathe a word of this to Eris. She’d want to go if she knew. Or, wait—Eris was a mature adult, now. She was far more logical and accommodating than she was in her spoiled princess days. She might want to go deep down, but she wouldn’t demand it. Right?

blocks.text: “It does,” said Roxy. “I hear it’s quite dangerous. It’s one of the Three Great Dungeons, in fact.”

blocks.text: “I wish I could go.”

blocks.text: “Let’s see… I think with our current members, we could get pretty far in. Rudy doesn’t like labyrinths too much, though. He lost Paul in one, after all…”

blocks.text: Roxy shut her down for me.

blocks.text: “What about you, Sylphie?”

blocks.text: “Hm?”

blocks.text: I turned my head to see that Eris tossed the question to Sylphie, who was playing with the baby in the carrier on my back.
blocks.html: I turned my head to see that Eris tossed the question to Sylphie, who was playing with the baby in the carrier on my back.

blocks.text: “Are you into labyrinths at all?”
blocks.html: “Are you into labyrinths at all?”

blocks.text: “Hmm… I suppose not. My children are more important to me right now.”
blocks.html: “Hmm… I suppose not. My children are more important to me right now.”

blocks.text: Sylphie reached a hand out and stroked Sieg’s head as she answered. Her tone was nonchalant. It sounded like her mental health was starting to recover.

blocks.text: No, that was a short-sighted way of thinking. I couldn’t assume from the surface. I needed to rebuild her trust. Back when Paul had the affair that got Lilia pregnant, it took him forever to regain Zenith’s trust. There was once a time when I didn’t understand why Zenith stayed angry for so long, or why she didn’t just forgive him. Now, I understood; it was because Paul only reacted to what he saw on the surface, and only groveled until he got what he wanted.

scenes.location: Outside the skyfolk city of Aluce, Divine Continent

blocks.text: It was evening when we saw the city.
blocks.html: It was evening when we saw the city.

blocks.text: “Is that Aluce?”
blocks.html: “Is that Aluce?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “It seems kind of…humble.”
blocks.html: “It seems kind of…humble.”
blocks.speaker: Roxy

blocks.text: Roxy wasn’t kidding. All we saw across the plain was a series of houses built from rock, soil, and bone, all surrounded by a rather low fence. There were no fortified ramparts—a rarity for towns in this world. But maybe they had the right idea. A wall of any height wouldn’t do much to stop monsters that could fly. Still, was it wise to have no line of defense for your city?

blocks.text: I had my doubts as I approached the fence, but as I did… How to describe it? I felt as though a film had been placed over the town. It was like looking at the town through a sheet of glass.

blocks.text: “Looks like a barrier. A big one, at that.”
blocks.html: “Looks like a barrier. A big one, at that.”
blocks.speaker: Roxy

blocks.text: Upon hearing Roxy’s words, my understanding finally caught up with how the town was actually protected. Of course. There was no way it’d be left completely defenseless.

blocks.text: “Think they’ll let us in?” Sylphie asked.

blocks.text: “Hard to say,” I answered, approaching the barrier. “Orsted didn’t say anything about this.”
blocks.html: “Hard to say,” I answered, approaching the barrier. “Orsted didn’t say anything about this.”

blocks.text: Then again, not many of my acquaintances knew much about the skyfolk to begin with. You didn’t see skyfolk on other continents, so I had no idea what they were like. Were they exclusionary, or were they friendly toward other races?

blocks.text: Sylvaril was pretty much the only skyfolk I’d met, and given that she didn’t seem to regard me with much favor, that colored my assumptions. On the other hand, she was plenty lenient with people Perugius held in high regard, like Zanoba. Maybe it wasn’t as bad as I feared.

blocks.text: We came to an edge of the barrier alongside a fenced portion of the town. Barriers in this world typically acted like walls, cordoning off a specified area. That said, barriers could act entirely differently on the Divine Continent. Like, maybe they would deliver an electric shock on contact that fried you to a crisp…

blocks.text: If we raised our voices from outside the barrier, would it reach anyone inside the town? From what we could see, the inside of the fence was just farmland.

blocks.text: Hold on, did skyfolk even make farms? Well, I guess they did. It’s not like people with wings didn’t need to eat. Even that telepathic race that lived deep in the Demon Continent still farmed. Farming is key to life.

blocks.text: Never mind agriculture right now—how were we supposed to get in? My gut feeling would be to walk around the fence until we saw something that looked like an entrance, but there was no gap as far as I could see. There was nothing that seemed like a road either, so no clues there.

blocks.text: Actually, did a race of people who could fly even have the concept of making gaps like a gate to serve as an entrance? If you didn’t walk on the ground, you wouldn’t need to make roads. Did that mean we should have been looking for an entrance in the sky? I didn’t prepare a way for us to fly… Hmm. Destroying the barrier was starting to look like a better idea. We’d repair it later, of course, but we wouldn’t get anywhere until we got in.

blocks.text: We followed her gaze to see birds flying toward us from within the town. Even as far off in the distance as they were, I could tell they were pretty large. Probably about the size of people… Wait. Those were people. People with wings. Skyfolk.

blocks.text: The skyfolk descended upon us with no sound beyond the flaps of their wings. There were three of them. They wore simple robes of…well, it sounds strange to describe them as bird pelts, but something along those lines. They held spears in their hands. That was a bit unusual; the only race I’d seen use spears were the Superd.

blocks.text: “Ahem, do excuse us. I am Rudeus Greyrat. I came because Lord Perugius demanded that I have my child baptized here. Would you perhaps be acquainted with him?”

scenes.location: The skyfolk city of Aluce, Divine Continent

blocks.text: The city of Aluce was a bit plainer than I expected. The houses were indeed crafted from bone, rock, soil, and hay. Many of the buildings topped out at three or four stories. If I had to pick one thing that was particularly unusual, it was that I couldn’t see any staircases. I guess people here didn’t need them when they could fly.

blocks.text: I was expecting a bit more, you know, Roman-ish architecture, or maybe something a bit more angelic or a Heaven-ish vibe…but hey, the skyfolk were people who had wings. No more, no less. Aluce was probably a backwoods settlement on the edge of the continent, so it checked out.

blocks.text: There was no lodging here, and nobody spoke Human Tongue. That said, there was one word we could both understand: “Perugius.” Given how readily they welcomed us, these people must have held a deep gratitude toward the man.

blocks.text: We were led to some sort of meeting place. They brought us food, while a guy who resembled a village elder talked about something with a smile. Then he broke out the alcohol.

He was the baby that came for Perugius’s trial, so maybe they thought he had some good luck that would rub off on them.

blocks.text: I might have felt a bit unnerved by such lavish treatment under normal circumstances, but they seemed to have good intentions, so I accepted their welcome at face value and lodged for the night at the gathering hall.
blocks.html: I might have felt a bit unnerved by such lavish treatment under normal circumstances, but they seemed to have good intentions, so I accepted their welcome at face value and lodged for the night at the gathering hall.

blocks.text: That evening, after putting Sieg to sleep, I talked a bit with Sylphie.
blocks.html: That evening, after putting Sieg to sleep, I talked a bit with Sylphie.

blocks.text: “Turns out this place is pretty normal,” said Sylphie.
blocks.html: “Turns out this place is pretty normal,” said Sylphie.
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: “Yeah. I expected some kind of uncharted natural wonder since it’s called the ‘Divine Continent,’ but everyone living here is just a regular person. Outside of the flying thing.”
blocks.html: “Yeah. I expected some kind of uncharted natural wonder since it’s called the ‘Divine Continent,’ but everyone living here is just a regular person. Outside of the flying thing.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “I’ve never left the Central Continent. Are the others normal, too?”
blocks.html: “I’ve never left the Central Continent. Are the others normal, too?”
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: Hearing that reminded me of the wild splendor of the Demon Continent. The northwestern edge of Biegoya. The residents there looked differently, talked differently, and lived in houses unlike anywhere else’s. Outside of that, yeah, they were pretty much the same.
blocks.html: Hearing that reminded me of the wild splendor of the Demon Continent. The northwestern edge of Biegoya. The residents there looked differently, talked differently, and lived in houses unlike anywhere else’s. Outside of that, yeah, they were pretty much the same.

blocks.text: “Yeah, I guess they are. Each place has some slightly different customs, though.”
blocks.html: “Yeah, I guess they are. Each place has some slightly different customs, though.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “Ranoa and Asura have some differences there, yeah…”
blocks.html: “Ranoa and Asura have some differences there, yeah…”
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: Sylphie went quiet after saying that. Her face was tense, as though she was deep in thought. She didn’t look depressed.
blocks.html: Sylphie went quiet after saying that. Her face was tense, as though she was deep in thought. She didn’t look depressed.

blocks.text: “Is something the matter?”
blocks.html: “Is something the matter?”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: “I was just thinking that nobody treated Sieg weirdly.”
blocks.html: “I was just thinking that nobody treated Sieg weirdly.”
blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

blocks.text: “Ah, yeah, they didn’t.”
blocks.html: “Ah, yeah, they didn’t.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: The skyfolk of the Divine Continent didn’t participate in the Laplace War. Their isolation on the Divine Continent allowed them to be the one race to escape Laplace’s invasion. Of course they wouldn’t fear the Superd. That was why the warrior people of the village still used spears, and why they didn’t show any reaction to Sieg’s or Roxy’s hair colors.

blocks.text: According to Orsted, long ago…as in, over four thousand years ago during the time of the second Human-Demon War, they despised demons. No matter how long-lived your race is, though, four thousand years is a lot of time. Generations and generations. That hatred must have withered away.

blocks.text: Wait… No, it was possible that hearing the word Perugius had made them careful not to show overt hostility.

blocks.text: “If only everyone could be like them,” said Sylphie. I saw her lips draw into a smile that looked almost forced.

blocks.speaker: Sylphiette

scenes.location: Aluce Hill, Divine Continent

blocks.text: THE NEXT MORNING, the villagers happily guided us as we departed the village. For some reason, they gave us a set of packed meals for everyone, some bundles of leaves that may have been medicine, and a carved wooden charm figure.
blocks.html: THE NEXT MORNING, the villagers happily guided us as we departed the village. For some reason, they gave us a set of packed meals for everyone, some bundles of leaves that may have been medicine, and a carved wooden charm figure.

blocks.text: Though I call it a figure, it was nothing complex—just a simple wooden stick with plumage (I think from a skyfolk) stuck to it. Maybe it was the idol of this land’s god, passed down throughout the ages. Like the Sky God. While it may have been simply crafted, its sheer pricelessness would have made Zanoba weep with joy.

blocks.text: “Thank you very much.”
blocks.html: “Thank you very much.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: I said my thanks, and while my words weren’t understood, my gratitude appeared to be. They responded to my parting words by folding up their wings and crossing their fists in front of their chests.
blocks.html: I said my thanks, and while my words weren’t understood, my gratitude appeared to be. They responded to my parting words by folding up their wings and crossing their fists in front of their chests.

blocks.text: Aluce Hill was a tranquil place. The breeze billowing down its gentle incline was chilly, but the weather was clear, and its slope was decorated with a garden of white flowers. Sieg was sleeping soundly, thanks to all, and the rest of us had to fight off a wave of drowsiness ourselves.

Sieg was sleeping soundly, thanks to all, and the rest of us had to fight off a wave of drowsiness ourselves.

blocks.text: “Fwah… Oh, right.”
blocks.html: “Fwah… Oh, right.”
blocks.speaker: Rudeus

blocks.text: All of us suddenly getting sleepy despite just waking from a good night’s rest couldn’t have been a coincidence. I gave everyone a Qikara Fruit that I’d prepared beforehand.
blocks.html: All of us suddenly getting sleepy despite just waking from a good night’s rest couldn’t have been a coincidence. I gave everyone a Qikara Fruit that I’d prepared beforehand.

blocks.text: I took another look at the garden of white flowers on the slope. The pollen released by those ferocious flowers had a strong soporific effect.
blocks.html: I took another look at the garden of white flowers on the slope. The pollen released by those ferocious flowers had a strong soporific effect.

blocks.text: When squinting even further, I could see a single creature lying in wait, camouflaged against the garden. It was a monster called the Heaven’s Glider. It hid among the sleep-inducing white flowers and attacked anyone who fell asleep after venturing too close. It was rather small compared to other monsters, only about two meters long. It looked like a furry lizard. Its forearms were webbed like a bat’s, and its tail had a venomous stinger. It was a more cautious monster than others and was known for never daring to move against prey that wasn’t asleep.

blocks.text: Yeah, you could call it a coward. Sieg was sound asleep, but the Heaven’s Glider didn’t attack. It let us pass.
blocks.html: Yeah, you could call it a coward. Sieg was sound asleep, but the Heaven’s Glider didn’t attack. It let us pass.

blocks.text: The sedative effect of the white flowers lasted for about one hour. According to Orsted, you’d never wake up from falling asleep in the garden, but the effects didn’t last long if you got away from them quickly.
blocks.html: The sedative effect of the white flowers lasted for about one hour. According to Orsted, you’d never wake up from falling asleep in the garden, but the effects didn’t last long if you got away from them quickly.

blocks.text: Still, Sieg was only a month old. Once we were far enough away, I cast an antidote spell on him for good measure. The Qikara Fruits had a strong stimulant effect, but giving that to an infant sounded dangerous.
